analysis.one_liner: Restricts airline control of airport gates and slots, opens gates to smaller carriers, caps reservation-system fees, and eases foreign airline investment.
analysis.headline: The bill won bipartisan sponsorship and two subcommittee hearings in 1991, but was never reported out of the House Aviation Subcommittee and never got a vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted several ways dominant airlines lock competitors out: hoarding airport gates and takeoff slots, paying inflated fees to airline-owned reservation systems, and blocking foreign investment in struggling U.S. carriers. It would have required the Transportation Secretary to approve transfers of gates, slots, and foreign-route certificates based on which deal most improves competition. It also required concentrated airports — where one or two carriers control 60% or more of the gates — to let smaller carriers use unused gates, sometimes at reduced rates, and set rules so airline-owned computer reservation systems could not bias displays or charge competitors unfair fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Travelers, who could see more competition and lower fares; smaller airlines and new entrants, who would gain access to gates at concentrated airports, unbiased listings on reservation systems, and arbitration of participant fees; and financially struggling U.S. carriers, which could sell up to 49% of voting stock to foreign investors under conditions designed to preserve U.S. control and national security.

how_it_helps.text: Bars major carriers from transferring more than 5% of an airport's gates or more than 5% of the slots at a high-density airport in a year without Secretary of Transportation approval, with approval standards favoring maximum competition [S2][S3].

Defines a concentrated airport as one where one or two carriers hold rights to 60% or more of the gates, and lets operators of such airports rent unused gates to smaller carriers at reduced rates for up to five years [S3].
Directs the Secretary to create a procedure to order a concentrated airport to let a petitioning smaller carrier use a gate during unused hours on terms comparable to incumbent carriers [S3].

Prohibits reservation-system vendors from ordering or emphasizing listings by carrier identity, from offering some carriers more functional booking capabilities than others, and from barring subscribers from using other systems [S3].
Caps subscriber contracts at one year, bans minimum-transaction-volume requirements and cancellation penalties, and lets airlines contest reservation-system fees through binding arbitration [S3].

Lets foreign investors buy more of a U.S. carrier's voting stock than the current 75% U.S.-ownership rule allows — down to a 51% floor — but only if the purchase keeps U.S. citizens in control, meets national-security and reciprocity conditions, and keeps the carrier flying [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Dominant airlines, which would face competition for gates and slots at the airports they dominate; the airline-owned computer reservation systems, which would lose biased displays, long lock-in contracts, and unreviewed fee increases; and sellers of gate rights, who could no longer transfer them freely.

drawbacks.text: The Secretary of Transportation would gain broad discretionary power to approve or deny gate, slot, and route-certificate transfers, and critics of such controls argue political decisions about airport access can substitute for markets and invite lobbying over every transfer [S3].

Restricting transfers of gates, slots, and foreign-route certificates could reduce the value of those assets and limit the ability of a failing carrier to raise cash by selling them, which in the bankruptcy-heavy early 1990s was a real concern for carriers trying to survive [S3].

Requiring foreign buyers to meet eight conditions, including reciprocity and a finding that no U.S. citizen would buy the stock on comparable terms, limits how much relief the foreign-investment provision actually provides to cash-starved carriers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer case was strong: in 1991 a handful of big carriers controlled gates and slots at key airports and owned the reservation systems that travel agents had to use, and the bill attacked both choke points directly. The main honest objection is that giving the Transportation Secretary case-by-case control over gate, slot, and route transfers trades market flexibility for regulatory discretion, and that in a wave of airline bankruptcies the ability to sell assets quickly mattered. Still, the anti-competitive practices it targeted — gate hoarding, biased screen displays, lock-in contracts, and unchallengeable fee hikes — were well documented, and the bill was designed to be relatively narrow.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Public Works and Transportation Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee, which held hearings in May 1991 but never reported the bill, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. James Oberstar introduced the bill on April 24, 1991, joined by three Republicans and one Democrat as cosponsors [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Public Works and Transportation on the day of introduction [S1].
It was referred to the Aviation Subcommittee on May 6, 1991 [S1].
The subcommittee held hearings on May 15 and May 22, 1991, but no further action was taken and the bill never reached the House floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dominant airlines kept control of gates, slots, and their reservation-system revenues, and travelers got no relief from the practices the bill targeted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dominant airlines and their reservation systems

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Aviation Subcommittee
against.role: Subcommittee, Committee on Public Works and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Held two hearings in May 1991 but never reported the bill to the full committee, keeping it from ever reaching the House floor.

against.name: Major U.S. airlines and airline-owned reservation systems
against.role: Dominant carriers and computer reservation system vendors
against.what_they_did: Had strong incentives to oppose the bill's gate-transfer limits and reservation-system fee arbitration, and the CRS rules in the bill responded to practices the industry was publicly defending.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — Oberstar plus one Democratic and three Republican cosponsors — and the bill died quietly in subcommittee rather than on a party-line vote.

industries.note: Carriers with revenues over $750 million would need government approval to transfer more than 5% of an airport's gates or a high-density airport's slots in a year, and dominant carriers at concentrated airports would have to share unused gates with smaller rivals. Their gate and slot hoarding at key hubs has long meant higher fares for travelers.

The big reservation systems were owned by major airlines and charged competing carriers fees while biasing what travel agents saw on screen. The bill would force neutral displays, cap contract terms, allow fee arbitration, and let subscribers switch systems.

Smaller carriers would get access to unused gates at concentrated airports, comparable terms from the airport, fair treatment and arbitration on reservation-system fees — the tools they needed to compete with dominant incumbents.

Foreign buyers could acquire up to 49% of the voting stock of a U.S. carrier, but only under strict conditions including U.S. citizen control, reciprocity, and a finding that no American buyer was willing to step in — aimed at keeping cash-starved carriers flying.
